data.content_ref: inline:The target conflates corroborability (an a priori logical property: the potential to pass severe tests) with corroboration (an a posteriori historical property: having actually survived tests). The claim is about a preference for 'better-corroborated' theories, but the mechanism only defends preferring 'higher empirical content (and thus higher corroborability).' Exposure to falsification is maximized by choosing a testable theory BEFORE testing; corroboration is a record of AFTER testing. So the mechanism justifies preferring more-falsifiable conjectures, not preferring theories that have already passed tests. Preferring a theory because it survived past tests is precisely using past performance as a forward-looking guide — the inductive inference the claim explicitly disclaims. Thus the target's own countercondition ('If the preference implies an expectation that the future will resemble the past, it fails') is triggered by the corroboration component, but the target never addresses this because it substitutes the distinct concept of corroborability in the mechanism.
